big: When Meena buys one share of a company, she becomes a very small owner of that business. If it earns well, she can gain. If it struggles, she can lose. Nobody promises her anything.

lines: So buying a share is like lending money to the company?
No. A lender is promised interest. An owner shares in profit and in loss. That is why a share can rise, fall, or even go to zero.

rows: A unit of ownership in a company
The regulated marketplace, such as NSE or BSE
A registered middleman who places your order
The regulator that sets the rules and protects investors
note: You do not trade with the company. You trade with other investors, through a broker, on an exchange.

title: Shares and markets
stops: A share makes you a part-owner of a company
A share promises a fixed return
SEBI is the regulator of the securities market
Any person can act as a broker without registration
caps: A shareholder owns a small part of the business.
Returns depend on how the business and the market do. Nothing is promised.
SEBI registers intermediaries and writes the rules for exchanges and brokers.
A broker must be registered. Check before you open an account.

q: Rohan buys 10 shares of a listed company. What does he now own?
opts: A loan he has given to the company
A small part of the company
A fixed deposit with a set rate
A promise of fixed yearly income
why: A loan earns promised interest. A share does not, as it is ownership.
A share is a unit of ownership, so he is now a small part-owner.
A fixed deposit has a set rate and a bank behind it. A share has neither.
No share carries a promise of fixed income, since profits can change.

q: Where are listed shares bought and sold in India?
opts: Directly at the company's head office
At a bank branch counter only
On stock exchanges such as NSE and BSE
why: A company does not sell its listed shares across its own counter.
A bank counter does not match buyers and sellers of listed shares.
A jeweller has no role in trading listed shares.
Exchanges are regulated marketplaces where buyers and sellers meet openly.

q: A broker is found misusing client money. Which body can act on the broker?
opts: The company whose shares were traded
why: SEBI registers brokers and has the power to act when rules are broken.
A post office has no authority over a broker or the market.
The company is not responsible for a broker's conduct with clients.
A newspaper can report a case, but it cannot punish the broker.

q: Meena wants to open an account with a broker she found online. What should she check first?
opts: That the broker has a flashy website
That the broker promises quick profits
That the broker is registered with SEBI
That the broker offers a gift for signing up
why: A website can look good and still belong to an unregistered firm.
Promises of quick profits are a warning sign and not a mark of safety.
A broker must be registered, and the regulator's list shows whether it is.
A gift for signing up says nothing about whether the broker is genuine.

pts: A share is part-ownership of a company, with no promised return.
You trade on an exchange, through a registered broker.
SEBI is the regulator. Always check that a broker is registered.
